book.title: Competing Against Luck: The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice
book.author: Clayton M. Christensen, Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon, David S. Duncan

chapters.title: The Milk Shake Dilemma
chapters.hook: Nella passes the muffin case because the cup has to last until the tunnel clears.
chapters.counterintuition: Most teams assume demand hides inside the product or the customer profile. It rarely does. The clearer signal is the moment of struggle that makes one option feel hireable.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one thing you bought today and write the exact moment before the choice: time, place, what felt hard, and what else you almost used.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A product makes sense only after you name the progress it is hired to create in a specific circumstance, then compare it with every substitute that could serve that same moment.

breakdown.fastRead: At 6:42 a.m., a commuter stands in front of muffins, bananas, coffee, and a thick shake. The category says dessert. The drive says breakfast tool. She needs one hand free, ten minutes of quiet, and something that will not dust her coat with crumbs. That is the milk shake lesson in miniature. Choice becomes less mysterious when you stop staring at the object and ask what progress the situation demands. The product is not competing only with similar products. It is competing with every option that could make the same morning easier.
breakdown.deepRead:
The useful question is not, who buys this product. It is, what job does the buyer need done right now. A product description can be accurate and still explain almost nothing. A thick drink in a cup is just a thick drink until the commute, hunger, boredom, and one-handed constraint arrive. Then the same drink becomes a practical answer.

Picture a parent at 2:18 p.m. at a Little League snack bar. The child wants a grape slush, and the parent is not buying refreshment. He is buying a small yes after six no answers all week, with a manageable spill risk and a visible sign that he is not the strict parent every inning. That job has a different shape from the morning drive, even if the receipt still says drink.

The move is to start with circumstance. Name the push in the old situation, the progress desired, and the real substitutes on the table. A banana, a bagel, a skipped breakfast, and a shake can all compete if the job is surviving a dull drive with clean hands. The limit is important: one vivid story does not explain every sale. The job must be tied to the moment, not stretched across every buyer because the product name matches.
breakdown.fullRead:
The milk shake case matters because it catches a common research error at the moment it feels sensible. A company asks customers what they want changed about a product. Sweeter, thicker, cheaper, larger, smaller. The answers sound useful, and some of them may be. But they arrive after the real causal question has already been skipped. Why did this buyer choose this option in the first place.

Jobs thinking changes the unit of analysis. The buyer is not a profile floating through a store. The buyer is a person in a circumstance trying to make progress. In the morning example, the circumstance carries much of the explanation. The commute is long. Breakfast has to be portable. The driver wants something to occupy the ride, hold off hunger, and stay clean in a car. Those constraints make the shake strong for reasons that are invisible if the team only asks about flavor.

Now change the moment. A parent buys a similar drink for a child after practice. The functional need is smaller. The social need is larger. The parent wants a simple treat, a low-conflict yes, and a purchase that ends the stop without a debate over candy, soda, or a toy. Same product, different progress. This is why the method has to separate occasions before it averages data. Averages can smooth away the very pressure that explains the choice.

The practical test is competition. Once the job is visible, rivals no longer sit only inside the category. A morning shake may compete with a banana, a bagel, a protein bar, black coffee, or nothing at all. A parent-child treat may compete with ice cream, a dollar store toy, a promise to stop later, or a small lecture about patience. The buyer's situation defines the field.

The objection is fair: people do care about product features. They do. Thickness, cup shape, price, and taste still matter. The point is sequence. Features matter after the team understands the job they must serve. Without that job, improvements become guesses wearing data. With it, the team can ask whether a change helps the specific progress that made the product worth hiring. The job is the standard that turns product work into judgment.

examples.title: Nella reaches past the muffins before the ferry horn

planSpec.stakes: feature research misses the one-handed commute job
planSpec.requiredBeat: she reaches past neat breakfast items because the drive needs a one-handed, slow option

examples.scenario: Nella grips a paper cup sleeve at 6:42 a.m. inside the Red Hook ferry kiosk, her laptop bag sliding off one shoulder while the horn groans outside. The muffin case is bright and full, but crumbs will land on her black coat before the tunnel. A banana will be gone before the bridge. She points to the thick vanilla shake, not because she wants dessert, but because it will keep one hand busy until the meeting deck loads. The clerk is already reaching for the lid.
examples.whatToDo: Study the moment around Nella's choice before asking which flavor she prefers. List the drive, the hunger, the free hand, and the substitutes she rejected at the counter.
examples.whyItMatters: The cup wins because it fits the commute better than nearby breakfast items. The job redraws the market around the situation, not around the menu category.

examples.title: Isao names the slush job at field three

planSpec.stakes: same product hides a parent-child progress job
planSpec.requiredBeat: he names the social job behind a treat, not the product preference

examples.scenario: Isao wipes grape slush from the snack-bar counter at 2:18 p.m. while his daughter Mina waits with cleats in one hand. "You hate sticky drinks," the cashier says. Isao laughs and looks toward field three, where Mina struck out twice and still carried the bats. "I am not buying grape," he says. "I am buying five quiet minutes where she knows I saw her try." He must decide whether to treat the order like a flavor request or like a small repair after a hard game.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the flavor from the progress. Ask what the purchase is helping Isao say to his daughter, then judge alternatives by whether they deliver that small social repair cleanly.
examples.whyItMatters: The same drink can do a different job after a game than it does on a commute. Treating both as beverage demand erases the reason each one wins.

examples.title: Briony pauses the cancellation reel at the backpack

planSpec.stakes: demographic grouping hides the moment of struggle
planSpec.requiredBeat: she must decide whether to group buyers by profile or by struggling moment

examples.scenario: Briony freezes the video at 11:06 a.m. in the research room, the customer on screen still wearing a bike helmet and a wet backpack. Three cancellers are all thirty-something designers, and the slide template wants one persona. But each quit at a different moment: tax season, a train platform, a handoff with a contractor. Her cursor hovers over the segment label. She must decide whether to sort by who they are or by the moment where the product stopped helping.
examples.whatToDo: Build the analysis around the struggling occasion. Keep the helmet, train platform, and contractor handoff separate until the progress each buyer needed is clear.
examples.whyItMatters: Similar profiles can hide different jobs. If Briony averages the people first, the team may optimize for a persona that never faced one common problem.

examples.title: Kavi guesses caffeine and the receipt tape answers twice

planSpec.stakes: one product category conceals two demand stories
planSpec.requiredBeat: his prediction by category fails when two occasions reveal two jobs

examples.scenario: Kavi tears the receipt tape at 4:37 p.m. beside the campus store register, certain the new mango smoothie is winning because students want caffeine-free sweetness. He predicted one afternoon crowd. The tape says otherwise. At 7:50 a.m., rushed lab partners buy it with protein bars and leave fast. After club meetings, students split one cup and linger by the window. Kavi has to decide before tomorrow's order whether one smoothie is one job or two.
examples.whatToDo: Let the reveal split the demand. Track the rushed morning hire and the lingering social hire as separate occasions before changing stock, size, or price.
examples.whyItMatters: A single SKU can hide more than one progress story. If Kavi forces one explanation, the next stocking decision will serve neither moment well.

examples.title: Greer finds the missing dinner job after the redesign

planSpec.stakes: product polish failed because the job was misread
planSpec.requiredBeat: she sees the team improved the product while missing the after-work job

examples.scenario: Greer sits at her kitchen island at 9:11 p.m., foil seals and customer notes spread around a cold skillet. Her meal-kit team added prettier cards, fresher herbs, and QR videos, yet renewals fell in February. In the notes, tired parents mention 6:20 p.m., math homework, and one pan already soaking. The postmortem lands hard: they improved cooking theater when buyers had hired the kit to make a weeknight feel survivable.
examples.whatToDo: Rewrite the failure around the after-work circumstance. Ask what the kit was hired to remove, compress, or calm during that narrow dinner window.
examples.whyItMatters: Better product attributes can still miss the job. The redesign lost because it added polish to the wrong part of the buyer's evening.

examples.title: Selah changes the locker-room snack pile

planSpec.stakes: naming the job changes the substitute set
planSpec.requiredBeat: she moves from favorite snacks to job-fit snacks after naming the real shift need

examples.scenario: Selah lines up crackers, oranges, and a thermos on the locker-room bench at 6:05 p.m. before the Tuesday night shift. Last month she packed whatever tasted good and hit the vending machine at 2:00 a.m. After watching herself chart with sticky fingers and a crashing stomach, she names the real job: stay steady through admissions without a mess at the desk. The orange goes back in the bag. The thermos stays.
examples.whatToDo: Choose against the shift job, not against snack preference. Name the messy desk, the 2:00 a.m. dip, and the need for slow energy before judging options.
examples.whyItMatters: The clearer job changes what counts as good. Selah is not choosing the best snack in general, she is choosing the best answer to a specific night.

reviewCards.front: A customer praises the product but keeps using a clumsy workaround. What should you retrieve first?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the situation before the quote. Ask when the workaround appears, what progress it protects, and which anxiety keeps the customer from switching cleanly.

reviewCards.front: You see one product used in two different moments. What move keeps the analysis sharp?
reviewCards.back: Separate the moments. A shared product name can hide different jobs, different substitutes, and different standards for what good means.

reviewCards.front: A roadmap debate turns into feature ranking. How do you bring back the commute job?
reviewCards.back: Put the buyer's struggling moment on the table, name the progress being hired, and judge each feature by whether it helps that movement happen.

reviewCards.front: A team has a beautiful story from one buyer. What question prevents overreach?
reviewCards.back: Ask which evidence repeats across similar circumstances and which details are local. A job story earns power through repeated hires, not through one vivid quote.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice reading demand from the situation before judging the product. The skill is to name the progress a person is trying to make, list the substitutes already in play, and test whether your offer helps that progress better than the current workaround.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a meeting starts ranking feature ideas, then write the buyer's exact moment of struggle at the top of the notes and force every option to answer how it improves the commute job.
If you abandon a tool that looked sensible, then pause for one minute and name what the old habit protected before you replace it with another polished option.
If a repeated purchase feels oddly satisfying or oddly disappointing, then write the time, place, substitute, and desired progress before deciding what to buy next.
If someone asks for a surface fix, then ask what situation made the request urgent and what would feel better after the fix works.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, catch one choice while it is happening. Write the clock time, the place, the old workaround, the anxiety around switching, and one sentence naming the progress you are hiring the option to deliver.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, interview one person about a recent switch. Do not start with features. Reconstruct the moment, the push away from the old way, the pull of the new way, and the substitute they almost kept.

chapters.title: Progress, Not Products
chapters.hook: Oona stares at a soaked ceiling tile and does not want a better repair app.
chapters.counterintuition: Most people assume progress means a functional upgrade. But actually the hire often includes social relief, less embarrassment, and a safer feeling of control.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one current frustration as a before and after: what situation are you in now, and what would feel noticeably better ninety seconds later?
chapters.keyTakeaway: Progress is the movement a person wants from a strained current state to a better one, including the practical, social, and emotional change the moment demands.

breakdown.fastRead: Oona stands under a wet ceiling tile at 7:28 a.m. and wants the leak handled before her landlord blames the washer again. A repair app, a phone call, a neighbor's wrench, and a bucket are all possible answers. The product label does not explain the hire. The progress does. She wants the drip stopped, but she also wants to feel believed, not foolish, when she reports it. Progress is the movement from this strained state to a better one. It can be practical, social, and emotional at the same time.
breakdown.deepRead:
Progress is more precise than desire. It names a movement from a current circumstance toward a better state. The current state has friction, risk, delay, or discomfort. The better state has a shape the buyer can recognize. A person may want the form filed, the leak stopped, the child calmer, the invoice paid, or the room less humiliating.

At 5:46 p.m., Dima clips a cape around a customer before a reunion. The customer asks for the same haircut as last time, but keeps touching the thin spot near his crown. A literal reading says, repeat the cut. A progress reading says, help him walk into the reunion without feeling watched. The scissors are functional. The job is larger.

This is why social and emotional forces are part of the work, not decorations around it. A tool that solves the task while making the buyer feel exposed may still lose. A service that gives less technical power but lets the buyer feel capable may win. The limit is that progress must stay tied to a circumstance. If the phrase gets inflated into happiness, freedom, or a better life, it stops guiding design. Name the before, name the after, and keep both close enough to observe.
breakdown.fullRead:
A product is a thing. Progress is a change. That difference sounds small until a team tries to explain why a customer chooses one answer over another. The thing can be described from the company's side: features, package, speed, price, materials, interface. The change has to be described from the buyer's side: what is wrong now, what would feel better, and what has to be protected while the buyer moves.

The movement often has three layers. Functional progress is the obvious layer. The leak stops. The form gets filed. The car starts. Social progress is about how the buyer can appear to other people. The parent feels responsible. The new employee does not look lost. The patient does not feel like a burden. Emotional progress is about the internal state that changes when the answer works. The buyer feels calmer, less exposed, more ready, or less stuck.

Good innovation work does not rank those layers too early. It listens for how they combine in the live circumstance. Rhea, an HR lead, may think an enrollment tool is about completing benefit forms. Then she watches an employee stand by the printer at 3:03 p.m., pay stub in hand, afraid to ask whether the dependent-care account means she has been leaving money behind for years. Completion matters, but shame is blocking the hire. A tool that only speeds the form may miss the progress.

The useful test is concreteness. A claim such as customers want confidence is too broad unless the team can point to the situation where confidence is missing and describe what would change. Confidence before a job interview, after a medical bill, during a first gym visit, or in front of a teenager's math homework are not the same job. Each has different substitutes and different signs of success.

This also explains why buyers can seem inconsistent. The same person may pick the cheapest option in one setting and a premium option in another. The person did not become irrational. The progress target changed. When the team can see that movement clearly, product decisions become less like preference guessing and more like helping the buyer cross a specific gap.

examples.title: Oona looks past the repair app under the wet tile

planSpec.stakes: functional repair misses dignity and trust
planSpec.requiredBeat: she hires speed, dignity, and relief, not a generic repair app

examples.scenario: Oona presses a cereal bowl under the drip at 7:28 a.m. in the third-floor laundry room, water darkening the ceiling tile above her shoulder. The building app promises faster maintenance, but the last ticket came back marked user error. Her thumb rests on the upload button while the washer thumps behind her. She does not only need a plumber. She needs a record that makes the landlord believe her before the stain reaches the hallway.
examples.whatToDo: Define the progress as more than leak repair. Capture the need for evidence, speed, and dignity before deciding whether the app, a call, or a neighbor witness is the right answer.
examples.whyItMatters: The practical fix and the emotional relief are joined in this moment. If the service only handles water, it may still fail the job Oona is hiring it to do.

examples.title: Dima hears the reunion inside the haircut request

planSpec.stakes: literal requests hide social progress
planSpec.requiredBeat: he hears the customer wants to feel unexposed at a reunion

examples.scenario: Dima snaps the black cape at 5:46 p.m. in the barber chair, the neck strip tight against Arun's collar. "Same as last time," Arun says, then taps the thin patch near his crown and glances at the mirror. "My cousins are all coming tonight." Dima sets the clippers down. "So we are not just matching last time," he says. "We are making sure the first joke is not about your hair." Arun exhales and has to decide whether to admit that is exactly the job.
examples.whatToDo: Listen past the requested cut. Ask what room Arun is walking into and what he wants to avoid feeling there, then choose the haircut against that social moment.
examples.whyItMatters: The service is not only removing hair. It is helping a customer cross a public threshold with less exposure, and that changes what good work means.

examples.title: Rhea stops at the dependent-care question by the printer

planSpec.stakes: completion metrics ignore emotional friction
planSpec.requiredBeat: she must decide whether functional completion is enough when shame blocks action

examples.scenario: Rhea stands beside the HR printer at 3:03 p.m., warm forms curling into the output tray while an employee holds a pay stub with two fingers. The new enrollment tool has a clean progress bar and no errors. Still, the employee whispers, "If I ask about dependent care, will payroll know I messed this up last year?" Rhea's pen hovers over the vendor scorecard. She must decide whether completed forms prove the job is done.
examples.whatToDo: Score the tool against the shame in the moment. Add private guidance, plain examples, and a way to check choices without broadcasting confusion.
examples.whyItMatters: A technically smooth flow can fail if the buyer feels exposed. Progress includes reaching the better state without paying a social cost that blocks the switch.

examples.title: Quincy learns why first-timers rent the dull shoes

planSpec.stakes: product prediction misses beginner progress
planSpec.requiredBeat: his product-based prediction misses progress from nervous first-timers

examples.scenario: Quincy counts rental shoes at 9:20 a.m. by the climbing gym cubbies, sure the bright new performance pairs will move first. They sit untouched. The scuffed gray shoes vanish before ten. On the waiver desk, first-timers keep asking whether they will look ridiculous. The reveal stings: they are not hiring rubber. They are hiring permission to try badly. Quincy has to decide before the next order whether better means grippier or less intimidating.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the rental choice as beginner progress. Preserve shoes, signage, and staff cues that make a nervous first attempt feel normal, then improve performance second.
examples.whyItMatters: The best technical product may lose when it raises the social cost of starting. The job is entry into the activity, not only grip on the wall.

examples.title: Maren reads the unopened reports after renewals fall

planSpec.stakes: measures missed the parent progress job
planSpec.requiredBeat: she sees parents hired confidence before grades

examples.scenario: Maren sits at 8:41 p.m. with unopened progress reports fanned across her dining table, each one printed on heavy cream paper. Spring renewals are down, even though scores rose. Parent emails mention car rides, tears before algebra, and not knowing what to say at conferences. The postmortem becomes uncomfortable. Families did not hire the tutoring center only for points. They hired a way to stop feeling helpless at the kitchen table.
examples.whatToDo: Rebuild the renewal review around parent progress. Track confidence in helping, calmer homework starts, and clearer conference language alongside test gains.
examples.whyItMatters: Grades are part of the job, but not the whole movement. If parents still feel useless at home, the service has not delivered what kept them paying.

examples.title: Ruth books therapy before the elevator reaches one

planSpec.stakes: appointment optimization misses recovery momentum
planSpec.requiredBeat: she stops optimizing appointment time and starts hiring momentum

examples.scenario: Ruth waits outside the clinic elevator at 12:14 p.m. on Wednesday, discharge sheet folded into a white square in her coat pocket. Before the knee flare, she booked therapy by cheapest slot and shortest drive. After three skipped weeks, she notices the real job: leave the appointment with enough momentum to do the exercises before doubt returns. She chooses the therapist who sends her straight to the small practice room, even though parking is worse.
examples.whatToDo: Choose the appointment against recovery momentum. Value the handoff into practice, the reminder before fear returns, and the setting that makes the next rep happen.
examples.whyItMatters: The practical task is not booking a slot. It is moving from intention to repeated action while pain and doubt are still loud.

chapters.hook: Harun watches the cough-syrup shelf lose to a thermos, honey, and a text from home.
chapters.counterintuition: Most teams assume a famous case should be copied. But actually the method travels only when each new setting is read on its own terms.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick a market far from your own and write one struggling moment in it. Identify the current workaround before naming any product idea.

breakdown.fastRead: Harun sees a shopper leave the cough-syrup shelf with honey, lemons, and a thermos. The store lost a medicine sale, but the job did not vanish. The shopper wanted to get through a night shift without sounding sick on calls. Jobs thinking works in pharmacies, schools, freight yards, kitchens, and churches because the unit is not a category. It is progress under pressure. The danger is copying one old story. The discipline is reading each new struggle with fresh eyes.
breakdown.deepRead:
A useful idea has to travel without becoming a copy machine. The milk shake case is memorable, but the method matters more than the object. In the wild, the same lens can explain why someone chooses a study room, a cheap repair, a rideshare, a paper checklist, or a neighbor's borrowed ladder. The common structure is not the product. It is a person trying to move from one state to another under specific pressure.

At 1:12 p.m., Miko unlocks a school instrument closet while a sixth grader says she wants the dented trumpet, not the shiny one. The shiny one is better. The dented one belonged to last year's section leader, and choosing it makes the first rehearsal less lonely. The job is not instrument quality alone. It is entering a group without feeling like a visitor.

The portable move is to ask the same disciplined questions, not to expect the same answer. What struggle is active. What alternatives are real. What anxiety slows the switch. What would count as progress in this setting. The limit is local evidence. A team that imports a story from another market without field observation is not using the method. It is borrowing confidence.
breakdown.fullRead:
Jobs thinking is strongest when it crosses categories and still keeps its feet on the ground. A pharmacy choice, a school choice, a shipping choice, and a home choice can all be read through progress. That does not mean they share one hidden script. It means each contains a circumstance where a person is trying to make a situation better and has more than one possible way to do it.

This matters because category logic trains teams to look sideways at familiar rivals. A cough remedy competes with other cough remedies. A tutoring service competes with other tutoring services. A museum membership competes with other memberships. In the wild, the buyer's real field is wider and stranger. Honey and a thermos can compete with cough syrup. A YouTube explainer can compete with tutoring. A Saturday soccer schedule can compete with a museum membership. The job makes those comparisons reasonable.

Portability also demands humility. If a team hears one vivid story and pastes it across every setting, the insight becomes brittle. The new setting has its own timing, shame, workarounds, constraints, gatekeepers, and measures of success. The buyer may be trying to avoid waste, gain permission, save face, calm a child, pass a shift, or look competent in front of peers. Those differences matter.

Eleri, watching a freight dispatch board at 4:08 a.m., might learn more from the drivers' handwritten parking notes than from the official route software. The software is the category product. The notes show the job: arrive with enough certainty to sleep before the next legal driving window closes. That kind of evidence appears only when the team studies the local struggle.

The objection is that a theory that travels everywhere may explain nothing. That is fair if the theory becomes vague. The answer is specificity. A jobs claim should name the circumstance, the push away from the old way, the pull of the new option, the anxiety, the habit, and the substitute set. If it cannot do that, it has not earned the right to guide design.

So the method travels as a questioning pattern. It does not travel as a canned answer. The team can use it in any domain, but it must make the buyer's situation prove the point again each time.

chapters.title: Job Hunting
chapters.hook: Ilya finds the job in a wad of refund slips beside washer twelve.
chapters.counterintuition: Most teams assume customers will state the opportunity directly. But actually the best clues often appear in delays, workarounds, and tolerated pain.
chapters.tryThisNow: Spend one minute looking for a workaround near you: taped cord, copied note, backup app, saved box. Write what struggle it is carrying.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Job hunting means looking for moments where current answers break down enough that people improvise, postpone, complain, or pay a cost to make progress anyway.

breakdown.fastRead: Ilya does not find the laundromat chance in a survey. He finds it in refund slips, wet socks, and a taped sign on washer twelve. Job hunting starts where the current answer strains. People work around, delay, overpay, ask a friend, or tolerate shame because no better path feels safe yet. Those behaviors are stronger evidence than a wish list. Look for the old setup failing in public, then ask what progress the person is still trying to protect.
breakdown.deepRead:
Job hunting begins before the customer turns struggle into a feature request. By the time someone asks for a button, a discount, or an app, the original pressure may already be translated into solution language. The hunt has to move upstream. Watch the moment where the old way becomes awkward, risky, slow, costly, or humiliating.

At 8:02 a.m., Freya sits beside a bus rider who has three transit apps open and a paper timetable folded into his phone case. He is not asking for another map. He is trying to arrive at work without being the person who is late again after daycare drop-off. The workaround stack shows urgency, anxiety, and the substitutes he trusts when each digital answer fails.

With the work in front of you, the move is to collect evidence from struggle. Record what people almost do, what they keep despite complaints, what they patch together, and what finally makes the old answer intolerable. The limit is complaint volume. A loud complaint is not automatically a job. A job needs circumstance, repeated pressure, real alternatives, and a clear better state. Without those, the team is chasing noise.
breakdown.fullRead:
A team that wants to find jobs on purpose has to stop waiting for customers to hand over perfect causal language. Customers usually speak from inside the current mess. They name the thing that annoyed them most recently. They request the feature they can imagine. They compare with the last option they tried. Those clues matter, but they are not the full job.

The strongest field evidence often looks indirect. A workaround means the buyer has already built a crude solution. A delay means the buyer wants progress but has not trusted any answer enough to switch. A tolerated cost means the current path is painful but still safer than the unknown. A substitute outside the category means the buyer's real frame is wider than the company's frame. Job hunting treats those signals as the map.

Chetan, behind a farm equipment counter at 5:17 a.m., may learn less from asking which seed monitor farmers want and more from watching them photograph the old display with a cracked phone before leaving. The phone is not a better monitor. It is a patch for remembering field sections while standing in mud with gloves on. That patch points to a job: keep enough confidence during a long morning that the wrong row does not get replanted.

Good hunting also asks what changed. Why now. What made the old way stop being acceptable this week. What anxiety keeps the buyer from switching today. What substitute nearly won. These questions turn observations into a causal story the team can test.

The objection is that every inconvenience can be made to sound like an opportunity. That is the trap. A weak job claim floats above evidence. A strong one has a scene, a tradeoff, a repeated workaround, and a substitute set. It also has a buyer who is already spending time, money, attention, reputation, or patience to make progress. If nobody is paying any cost, the hunt has probably found curiosity, not demand.

Job hunting is not a treasure hunt for clever anecdotes. It is disciplined attention to strain. The team follows the frayed tape, the backup spreadsheet, the second phone call, and the skipped purchase until the real progress battle comes into view.

chapters.title: How to Hear What Your Customers Don't Say
chapters.hook: Anja hears a mattress return in the pause before the receipt prints.
chapters.counterintuition: Most teams assume the customer quote is the insight. But actually the quote is evidence to interpret against behavior, hesitation, habit, and anxiety.
chapters.tryThisNow: Replay one recent complaint. Mark one push, one pull, one habit that kept the old way alive, and one anxiety that made change feel risky.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Strong customer listening treats words as evidence, then checks them against push, pull, habit, anxiety, and the visible tradeoffs in the buyer's situation.

breakdown.fastRead: Anja hears the customer say the mattress is too firm, but the pause before the receipt prints tells more. He asks whether pickup can happen after his partner leaves for work. The stated complaint is firmness. The job includes avoiding another bedroom argument. Listening for jobs is not transcription. It is interpretation tied to evidence. Watch what pushes the buyer away, what pulls a new option close, what habit holds the old way in place, and what anxiety makes switching feel dangerous.
breakdown.deepRead:
Customers often speak in the language available to them. They ask for a feature, blame a price, praise convenience, or offer a neat summary after the decision has already happened. Those words matter. They are just not enough. The listener has to reconstruct the forces around the switch.

At 11:19 a.m., Riko interviews a mother beside a folded stroller in a store aisle. She says she wants one that is lighter. Then she keeps describing subway stairs, a sleeping toddler, and the fear of strangers watching while she blocks the turnstile. The literal request is weight. The deeper job includes getting through public space without feeling trapped or judged.

The listening move is disciplined. Capture the quote, then attach it to behavior. What pushed the buyer away from the old answer. What pulled the new one into consideration. What habit makes the old answer hard to abandon. What anxiety makes the new answer risky. The limit is evidence. Do not invent a hidden story just because it sounds rich. A good interpretation can point to a scene, a tradeoff, and an action that confirms it.
breakdown.fullRead:
Customer listening fails when it treats words as either perfect truth or useless noise. Words are evidence. They need context. A buyer may say the mattress is too firm because firmness is the acceptable complaint. The less acceptable truth may be that the bed has become a nightly argument. A buyer may say an app is too expensive because price is easy to name. The harder truth may be fear of moving records, admitting confusion, or losing a habit that still feels safe.

The four-force lens gives listening a structure. Push is the dissatisfaction with the current situation. Pull is the attraction of a new possibility. Habit is the gravity of what the buyer already knows how to do. Anxiety is the worry that the switch will create a new problem. Real decisions often sit where those forces collide. A strong interview does not ask the customer to label them. It listens for stories, pauses, substitutions, delays, and contradictions that reveal them.

Melia, coding cancellation notes at 4:33 p.m., may find that users praise the tool and still quit during setup. If she only records positive sentiment, the team feels safe. If she listens for anxiety, she hears the repeated fear: what happens if the import breaks payroll on Friday. The words and the behavior diverge because the forces are fighting each other.

This kind of listening also protects teams from overvaluing articulate customers. The person who explains a choice cleanly may be giving a polished after-story. The quiet buyer who kept a receipt, delayed a switch for six months, and built a spreadsheet around a missing feature may show more causal evidence. The job is often clearer in what people do around the decision than in the sentence they use to justify it.

The objection is that interpretation can become mind reading. It can. The safeguard is visible evidence. A claim about anxiety should connect to a delayed purchase, a question asked twice, a fallback kept nearby, or a refusal to switch when the new option seems better. A claim about habit should connect to a routine the buyer protects. The listener earns the interpretation by showing where it appears in the world.

When listening works, the team stops asking customers to be theorists of their own behavior. It lets them be witnesses. The team then does the harder work: connect words, actions, and forces until the progress being hired becomes specific enough to design for.

chapters.title: Building Your Resume
chapters.hook: Ulric sees the kayak’s real resume in six muddy return cards clipped to a nail.
chapters.counterintuition: Most teams assume identity comes from positioning. But actually the market grants identity through repeated hires in similar circumstances.
chapters.tryThisNow: List three times someone chose the same product or service. Write the situation beside each one and circle the progress that repeats.
chapters.keyTakeaway: An offering’s resume is the pattern of jobs buyers repeatedly trust it to do, and that earned record should discipline promises, redesigns, and expansion.

breakdown.fastRead:
Ulric reads six muddy kayak return cards and notices the same note: safe first paddle with nervous guests. The rental shop thought its resume was fast boats and scenic water. The market had written a narrower one. A product's real identity is not what the team claims on a poster. It is what buyers keep hiring it to do when pressure repeats. One story can inspire. A pattern earns trust.

That is why the team should name the pattern before it writes the promise.
breakdown.deepRead:
A resume is an earned record. It says what a product or service has proven it can do in the situations buyers care about. Positioning can promise many things. The resume is narrower because it comes from repeated hires, not internal ambition.

At 4:40 p.m., Sonia wipes polish from her thumb in a shoe repair shop while a customer points to cracked boots. "You saved these before my last two inspections," he says. He is not buying leather work in general. He is hiring the shop to make him look squared away when his uniform gets judged. Three visits say more than any tagline.

Ulric's return cards also show what the team should ignore. One guest praised the color of the boats. Another liked the snack shelf. Those comments matter, but they do not yet form the resume. The repeated hire is the safer first paddle. The shop should protect that trust before chasing every compliment.

With the work in front of you, the move is to look for repetition with context attached. Who rehired, in what circumstance, after which pressure, and for what progress. If the same job appears across similar situations, the offering has earned that line on its resume. The limit is false unity. Repeated use does not prove one job if the circumstances differ. A team must separate patterns before it tells itself a proud story.
breakdown.fullRead:
Teams like to define products from the inside. They name capabilities, audiences, benefits, and brand attributes. Buyers write a different kind of record. They reveal what they trust by hiring the offering again when a familiar pressure returns. That record is the offering's resume.

The resume metaphor matters because it is earned. A person can claim a skill, but a resume is strongest when it shows repeated work under recognizable conditions. An offering works the same way. One strong story can point to a possible job. Many similar hires show what buyers have begun to rely on. The team should treat that reliance as strategic evidence.

This helps with focus. If a product is repeatedly hired to reduce anxiety before a high-stakes handoff, then a redesign that adds entertainment may distract from the earned job. If a service is repeatedly hired to make a novice feel capable in public, then expansion into expert features may ask buyers to trust something the service has not earned. The resume does not forbid growth. It asks whether growth extends an earned trust or demands a leap.

Basha, a school counselor at 2:27 p.m., may hear parents call the same hotline every grading cycle. The school may describe the hotline as information access. The repeated hire may be different: help me ask one specific question before I face my teenager tonight. If that is the resume, a giant resource portal could weaken the service by removing the human signal parents trust.

The caution is that repeated use can mislead when the team blends unlike jobs. A spreadsheet used every Friday by finance, every Tuesday by teachers, and every night by a caregiver may be one tool with three resumes. The team has to keep the circumstances attached. Otherwise it will claim broad trust where the market has granted only local trust.

Build the resume from repeated pressure, not from the loudest compliment. Write the job as a sentence with context attached: when this kind of buyer faces this kind of moment, they hire us for this kind of progress. Then test the next feature, message, or channel against that sentence. Does it strengthen the earned trust, or does it ask the market to believe a new claim?

The resume can grow, but growth has to be earned. A product may start by helping nervous beginners and later help confident users go farther. The bridge is proof. Without proof, expansion becomes wishful branding. With proof, the team can widen the promise without losing the job that made buyers come back.

The value of the resume is discipline. It disciplines messaging because the company should promise what buyers already rely on. It disciplines product work because changes should protect the job that earned the trust. It disciplines expansion because adjacent opportunities should be judged by whether the old resume helps or merely tempts the team. A market does not hand out identity all at once. It writes it through repeated hires.

chapters.title: Integrating Around a Job
chapters.hook: Arlen sees the discharge folder fail between the wheelchair and the pharmacy window.
chapters.counterintuition: Most teams assume insight is enough once the job is known. But actually the organization has to coordinate around that job or each local improvement can damage it.
chapters.tryThisNow: Trace one customer path across three handoffs. Mark where each team optimizes locally, then write the progress the whole path must protect.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A job becomes useful strategy only when product, service, operations, and support coordinate around the full progress buyers hired, not their separate internal targets.

breakdown.fastRead: Arlen watches a patient leave with clear discharge instructions, then get stuck at the pharmacy window because one form is missing. The nurse did her job. The printer did its job. The pharmacy followed policy. The patient's job still broke. Integration around a job means the organization judges handoffs by the progress the customer is trying to make, not by whether each department can defend its own step.
breakdown.deepRead:
A clear job can still fail in delivery. The customer experiences a path, while the organization often manages pieces. Product owns one part, operations another, service another, finance another. Each piece can improve its own metric and still make the buyer's progress worse.

At 12:22 p.m., Faye stands beside a cafe pickup shelf while a courier, a regular, and a parent with a stroller all look for unlabeled bags. The app team improved ordering speed. The kitchen improved batch output. The counter team reduced interruptions. The job, getting lunch without uncertainty, got worse because nobody owned the full moment.

The integration move is to make the job the shared reference point. Ask how each handoff helps or hurts the progress buyers hired. Then change incentives, scripts, tools, and staffing around that shared standard. The limit is scope. This is not a call for endless harmony. It is a demand that local wins lose priority when they weaken the full job.
breakdown.fullRead:
Jobs insight can create a new organizational problem. Once a team knows what buyers are hiring, the company may still be built to deliver something else. Departments carry their own metrics, calendars, budgets, and definitions of good work. Those structures are not malicious. They are just partial. The buyer does not experience them as partial. The buyer experiences one path that either helps progress happen or makes it harder.

Integration around the job means the job becomes the deciding reference point across functions. Product asks whether features protect the progress. Operations asks whether process choices keep the moment reliable. Service asks whether scripts reduce uncertainty at the right time. Finance asks whether rules create friction that defeats the hire. The work is practical, not poetic.

Jace, a university advisor at 3:45 p.m., can see this on a student transfer path. Admissions says the portal is complete. Financial aid says the award letter is correct. The registrar says credits are posted. The student still sits in the hallway unable to choose classes because nobody integrated around the job: make transfer feel real enough to plan Monday morning. Each office passed its checklist. The student's progress stalled.

Integration also protects against attractive local improvements. A faster kitchen can flood pickup shelves with unlabeled bags. A stricter fraud rule can make an insurance claim feel accusatory right when the customer needs stability. A beautiful app can move work onto a customer who was hiring relief from coordination. The right question is not, did this function improve. The right question is, did the buyer's progress become clearer, safer, faster, or more complete.

The objection is that companies cannot reorganize around every job. True. The discipline is to choose the jobs that define the offering's earned resume and integrate around those. Not every request gets a new structure. But the core hire deserves cross-functional protection because it is what buyers return for.

When integration works, tradeoffs become easier to argue. A department can still propose its local win, but it has to show how that win serves the full job. The job becomes the common language for refusing improvements that are good only from the inside.

chapters.title: Keeping Your Eye on the Job
chapters.hook: Asha sees a dinner rescue turn into a recipe contest at the pickup freezer.
chapters.counterintuition: Most teams assume alignment lasts after the job is named. But actually habit, metrics, and attractive side goals keep pulling work back inward.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take one current initiative and write the job it is supposed to protect. Cross out any metric or feature that no longer serves that progress.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Keeping focus on the job means testing every new feature, metric, exception, and process change against whether it sharpens or blurs the buyer's progress.

breakdown.fastRead: Asha watches a freezer fill with truffle risotto kits and realizes the grocery pickup service has drifted. Customers at first hired it to rescue dinner between work and bedtime. The new kits photograph well, but they ask for chopping, stirring, and a calm evening. Drift rarely announces itself. It arrives as fair fixes that serve internal hype more than the buyer's progress. The job has to stay an active filter.
breakdown.deepRead:
A company can learn the job and still lose sight of it. The danger is not always ignorance. Often it is drift. A familiar metric returns because it is easy to track. A side opportunity looks impressive. A function adds a feature because it can. Each move seems defensible alone. Together they bend the offering away from the progress buyers hired.

At 7:44 a.m., Brenna, a teacher, points at a cleaner attendance dashboard and says, "This makes my report prettier, but it makes morning harder." The old screen had one ugly button that told the office which children had not eaten breakfast. The redesign served reporting clarity and damaged the job of getting the first twenty minutes calm.

The move is repeated testing. Ask, does this change make the job sharper, easier, safer, or more complete for the buyer. If it mainly serves internal neatness, status, or measurement, treat it as suspect. The limit is not rigidity. Offers can evolve. But adaptation has to prove it still protects the hired progress.
breakdown.fullRead:
Job focus is hard to keep because organizations have memory. They remember categories, metrics, meetings, and habits more easily than they remember a customer's strained moment. After the first insight, old language creeps back. Roadmaps fill with features. Dashboards reward activity. Teams optimize the part they own. Nobody intends to abandon the job, but the offering slowly asks buyers to do more work, accept more confusion, or care about goals they never hired.

This drift can be subtle. A grocery service that was hired for weeknight rescue starts adding chef-driven kits. A school system that was hired for morning readiness starts optimizing reporting beauty. A bike repair shop that was hired for reliable commuting starts measuring accessory attachment. Each change can be defended as growth or improvement. The job test asks a colder question: did the buyer's desired progress improve.

Dillon, opening a bike shop at 8:16 a.m., may see the problem in one metric. The new goal rewards selling tune-up bundles. The commuter at the door needs the brake fixed before a hospital shift. If the bundle script delays that repair, the metric has become a rival to the job. The job should judge the metric, not the other way around.

Keeping focus also requires watching habits. Internal teams fall back to what they know how to discuss. Engineers discuss features. Sales discusses offers. Operations discusses throughput. chapters.title: The Jobs-Focused Organization
chapters.hook: Hugo sees the job lose when every dashboard in the room is green.
chapters.counterintuition: Most teams assume using jobs language means the organization has changed. But actually the change appears only when recurring decisions route through the buyer's progress.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take one recurring meeting and add a first agenda line: which buyer progress are we protecting today, and what tradeoff threatens it?
chapters.keyTakeaway: A jobs-focused organization keeps research, metrics, meetings, incentives, and tradeoffs anchored in the progress buyers hire, so judgment changes repeatedly.

breakdown.fastRead: Hugo stands in a handoff war room where every internal dashboard is green, while customers are still calling because medicine arrived after bedtime. A jobs-focused company is not one that knows the words. It is one whose repeated decisions are governed by the job. Metrics, handoffs, staffing, reviews, and tradeoffs all have to answer the same question: does this protect the buyer's progress. If the old incentives still win, only the words changed.
breakdown.deepRead:
A jobs-focused organization is built from repeated judgment. The job is no longer a research finding that lives in a slide. It becomes a standard for priorities, metrics, tradeoffs, service rules, and meetings. People can point to it when choosing what to protect and what to refuse.

At 9:32 a.m., Tirzah listens while fulfillment celebrates lower packaging cost and support reports a spike in cracked replacement parts. Both teams are right by their own measures. The buyer hired the company to restore a broken appliance before the weekend. Cheaper packaging that creates replacement calls is not a win through that lens.

The organizational move is to make the job consequential. Put it inside scorecards, escalation rules, roadmap reviews, and frontline scripts. Use it to settle conflicts between local goals. The limit is cosmetic adoption. Jobs language can spread quickly while decisions stay product-centered, function-centered, or metric-centered. The test is behavior under tradeoff, not vocabulary in a meeting.
breakdown.fullRead:
An organization becomes jobs-focused when the job changes how decisions are made again and again. Research is only the beginning. A team may discover a strong job, describe it beautifully, and still keep choosing through old categories. The sales target wins. The department metric wins. The roadmap habit wins. The customer progress becomes a phrase people respect but do not obey.

At the moment, the choice is visible. The deeper shift is governance. Which metrics matter. Which exceptions are allowed. Which tradeoffs get escalated. Which work gets funded. Which customer complaints are treated as urgent. A jobs-focused organization routes those questions through the progress buyers hire. This does not make every decision easy, but it gives the organization a shared standard that is outside its internal convenience.

Ira, leading a product review at 2:04 p.m., may see two dashboards. One says engagement is up because users open the app more often. The other says the same users take longer to finish the paperwork they hired the app to simplify. A product-centered organization celebrates engagement. A jobs-focused organization asks whether extra opens mean value or confusion. The job changes the interpretation of the metric.

On the calendar, this is why vocabulary is a weak test. A company can rename teams, add posters, and repeat the job in strategy decks while still rewarding the same behaviors as before. If approval paths, incentives, and resource fights do not change, the organization is not focused on the job. It is focused on sounding focused.

The objection is that organizations need many measures. They do. A jobs-focused organization still tracks cost, quality, growth, risk, and capacity. The difference is that those measures are interpreted through the buyer's progress when they conflict. Cost reduction is good unless it damages the hire. Engagement is good unless it signals confusion. Growth is good unless it pulls the offering away from the earned resume.

The value of this orientation is coherence. People in different functions can make local calls that still line up because they are using the same external standard. The job becomes a source of truth when pressure returns. Without that, jobs thinking remains an insight project. With it, the company develops a way to keep choosing on behalf of the progress that made customers come in the first place.

chapters.title: Final Observations About the Theory of Jobs
chapters.hook: Aster keeps the forecast pencil on the table because the job explains more, not everything.
chapters.counterintuition: Most teams want a theory to remove risk. But actually the value is better causal questioning, clearer evidence, and humbler judgment under uncertainty.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one decision as a job claim, then add the evidence that supports it and the one observation that would make you doubt it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Jobs Theory improves innovation judgment by explaining demand through progress in context, while still requiring evidence, tradeoffs, and humility about what remains uncertain.

breakdown.fastRead: Aster keeps a pencil beside the forecast because the job story is strong, not final. Jobs Theory does not make demand automatic. It gives teams a better lens: look at the progress a person seeks, the circumstance that makes it urgent, and the forces shaping the switch. That lens can reduce blind guessing. It cannot remove evidence, judgment, or tradeoffs. The best use of the theory is causal humility, not confidence theater.
breakdown.deepRead:
The final value of Jobs Theory is not that it makes innovation easy. It changes what a team tries to explain. Product categories, customer traits, and feature lists can all describe pieces of demand. They often fail to explain why a person chooses now, in this circumstance, with these substitutes available.

At 3:38 p.m., Bela listens to a founder declare that the job has been found, so the launch is safe. She points to the wall where interview notes, cancellation logs, and substitute photos are taped in separate columns. "Strong evidence," she says. "Not a guarantee." The job lens tells them what to test next, which tradeoffs matter, and which signals should change their mind.

That is the mature use of the theory. It makes behavior more intelligible by tying choice to progress in context. It also keeps teams honest by asking for evidence from the world. The limit is certainty. A job claim can be wrong, too broad, outdated, or true for only one occasion. Good teams use the lens to ask sharper causal questions, then keep testing.
breakdown.fullRead:
Jobs Theory earns its place because it shifts innovation away from weak explanations. A product label can say what was bought. A demographic profile can say who bought it. A feature ranking can say what people liked after the fact. None of those, by itself, explains why the choice happened. The stronger question is what progress the person was trying to make in a circumstance that made action feel necessary.

That question ties together the whole method. The opening product puzzle, the definition of progress, field observation, listening for forces, earned resumes, integration, sustained focus, and organizational judgment all depend on the same claim: demand becomes clearer when progress in context becomes the unit of analysis. The buyer is not a bundle of traits. The product is not the cause by itself. The circumstance and the desired movement give the hire its meaning.

Clem, facing a launch approval at 10:25 a.m., may have a beautiful job story supported by interviews. The wrong move is to treat that story as certainty. The right move is to ask what evidence would confirm or weaken it after launch. Do buyers switch without coaching. Do they abandon old substitutes. Do they rehire in the same circumstance. Do support calls match the predicted anxiety. The theory guides the test.

This matters because innovation work always contains uncertainty. Jobs Theory can reduce the fog by naming the forces at work and the alternatives that matter. It can help teams avoid category blindness, persona overconfidence, and feature-first noise. It can make competition more realistic and design criteria more concrete. But it cannot promise that every interpretation is right or that every execution will work.

The objection is that a theory with limits may feel less powerful. The opposite is true. A theory that admits limits is more useful because it tells teams where to keep looking. If a job claim lacks a concrete circumstance, it is too vague. If it ignores substitutes, it is too narrow. If it cannot predict behavior, it is not yet causal enough. If it never faces disconfirming evidence, it has become belief.

The best ending is therefore a working standard: explain demand through progress in context, design around the job that evidence supports, coordinate the organization to deliver it, and keep testing when reality pushes back. That does not defeat luck completely. It gives teams a better opponent.

examples.title: Aster leaves the forecast pencil beside the job notes

planSpec.stakes: theory improves explanation without certainty
planSpec.requiredBeat: she treats job evidence as stronger but not final

examples.scenario: Aster sets a yellow pencil beside the forecast sheet at 4:19 p.m. in the product planning room, interview cards taped across the wall and substitute photos clipped by binder rings. The job story is stronger than last quarter's persona deck. It still has blanks. Two buyers delayed for reasons nobody predicted. Aster needs to decide whether to lock the forecast as truth or mark the assumptions the launch must test first.
examples.whatToDo: Use the job story to sharpen the forecast, then write the assumptions that need proof. Track switching, rehire, and substitute abandonment after launch.
examples.whyItMatters: A causal lens reduces guessing, but it does not erase uncertainty. The team should know which parts of the job story reality still has to confirm.

examples.title: Quentin tells the founder strong evidence is not a guarantee

planSpec.stakes: confidence must stay tied to evidence
planSpec.requiredBeat: she names what the lens can and cannot prove

examples.scenario: Quentin stands at 3:38 p.m. beside a wall of interview notes, cancellation logs, and photos of homemade workarounds. "So we found it," the founder says, tapping the job statement. "Launch is safe." Quentin uncaps a red marker. "We found a better explanation," she says. "Now we test whether people switch when the old workaround is still sitting there." He looks at the marker, then the launch date. The decision in the room changes from belief to evidence.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the job claim as a testable explanation. Define the behavior that would prove it: switching, continued use, and fewer returns to the old workaround.
examples.whyItMatters: Jobs Theory should raise the quality of proof, not become a new way to declare victory before the market responds.

examples.title: Clem keeps one doubt on the launch approval page

planSpec.stakes: job story must face disconfirmation
planSpec.requiredBeat: he must decide whether a job story is certainty

examples.scenario: Clem sits at 10:25 a.m. with the launch approval page open, a fountain pen uncapped beside the signature line. The team has twelve interviews around the same job and a prototype customers praised. One test user still kept the old spreadsheet taped to her monitor. Clem's pen hovers above the approval box. He must decide whether the job story is enough to greenlight blindly or whether the first release needs a doubt column next to the plan.
examples.whatToDo: Approve only with a learning condition. Name the spreadsheet behavior as a disconfirming signal to watch and decide in advance what would trigger a redesign.
examples.whyItMatters: A strong job story becomes stronger when it can be tested. Ignoring the leftover substitute turns theory into faith.

examples.title: Dara predicts profiles and sees timing explain the switch

planSpec.stakes: profiles describe buyers less causally than circumstance
planSpec.requiredBeat: her profile prediction fails against circumstance evidence

examples.scenario: Dara sorts subscriber cards at 1:07 p.m. in the research lab, predicting age and income will explain who upgrades. The reveal comes from timestamps. Upgrades spike after lease renewals, new babies, and parents moving nearby. The same profiles split in opposite directions when the circumstance differs. Dara has to choose the next model before the director arrives: richer persona clusters or a map of the progress each timing event makes urgent.
examples.whatToDo: Model demand around triggering circumstances. Keep profiles as descriptors, but test timing, pressure, substitutes, and desired progress as the causal explanation.
examples.whyItMatters: Traits can describe buyers without explaining the hire. The switch becomes clearer when the event creates a new progress target.

examples.title: Hale postmortems the launch that treated insight as certainty

planSpec.stakes: overconfident job claim skipped evidence
planSpec.requiredBeat: he sees the team pushed theory past proof

examples.scenario: Hale sits at 8:36 p.m. on the warehouse floor, unsold sensor boxes stacked behind him like gray bricks. The team had a crisp job claim: help small restaurants avoid freezer loss. They skipped the part where owners distrusted weekend alerts from devices they could not repair. The postmortem is not that jobs thinking failed. The team treated a plausible job as finished proof and ignored the anxiety that would block installation.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the valid job from the untested switch. Revisit installation fear, repair trust, weekend alerts, and owner substitutes before relaunching.
examples.whyItMatters: A theory can point to demand and still miss adoption. Evidence has to include the forces that decide whether buyers will actually switch.

examples.title: Orly adds the doubt test to every innovation review

planSpec.stakes: better causal judgment needs recurring evidence checks
planSpec.requiredBeat: she changes reviews to include evidence and uncertainty

examples.scenario: Orly draws a black line down the whiteboard at 9:02 a.m. before the innovation review, markers lined up by color. Before, teams presented jobs, features, and revenue upside. After two confident misses, she adds two required boxes: evidence that would confirm the job and evidence that would make us doubt it. The room slows down. The theory stays useful because every claim now has to meet the world again.
examples.whatToDo: Add confirmation and doubt tests to the review. Make every job claim name the behavior that would strengthen it and the behavior that would force revision.
examples.whyItMatters: The lens improves judgment when it stays testable. A recurring evidence check keeps teams from turning a useful theory into a slogan.

questions.prompt: At 8:05 a.m., a bakery owner watches three regulars skip the croissants and buy plain coffee before the train doors close. The team is applying using Jobs Theory as a causal lens without treating it as certainty. Which next move best follows the jobs lens for this situation?
choices: Name the circumstance, the progress desired, and the substitutes already being used before changing features.
Rank customers by demographic similarity and average their requests into one roadmap item.
Ask the loudest buyer which feature would make the product seem more premium.
questions.explanation: The strongest answer starts with the pressured circumstance and the progress at stake. It treats observed behavior as evidence, then tests whether a real switch happens when that job is served better.

reviewCards.front: A customer praises the product but keeps using a clumsy workaround. What should you retrieve first?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the situation before the quote. Ask when the workaround appears, what progress it protects, and which anxiety keeps the customer from switching cleanly.

reviewCards.front: You see one product used in two different moments. What move keeps the analysis sharp?
reviewCards.back: Separate the moments. A shared product name can hide different jobs, different substitutes, and different standards for what good means.

reviewCards.front: A roadmap debate turns into feature ranking. How do you bring back causal demand judgment?
reviewCards.back: Put the buyer's struggling moment on the table, name the progress being hired, and judge each feature by whether it helps that movement happen.

reviewCards.front: A team has a beautiful story from one buyer. What question prevents overreach?
reviewCards.back: Ask which evidence repeats across similar circumstances and which details are local. A job story earns power through repeated hires, not through one vivid quote.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice reading demand from the situation before judging the product. The skill is to name the progress a person is trying to make, list the substitutes already in play, and test whether your offer helps that progress better than the current workaround.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a meeting starts ranking feature ideas, then write the buyer's exact moment of struggle at the top of the notes and force every option to answer how it improves causal demand judgment.
If you abandon a tool that looked sensible, then pause for one minute and name what the old habit protected before you replace it with another polished option.
If a repeated purchase feels oddly satisfying or oddly disappointing, then write the time, place, substitute, and desired progress before deciding what to buy next.
If someone asks for a surface fix, then ask what situation made the request urgent and what would feel better after the fix works.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, catch one choice while it is happening. Write the clock time, the place, the old workaround, the anxiety around switching, and one sentence naming the progress you are hiring the option to deliver.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, interview one person about a recent switch. Do not start with features. Reconstruct the moment, the push away from the old way, the pull of the new way, and the substitute they almost kept.
